abstract.t: This document specifies the Silent-Mail-Forwarding Prevention Standard (SMFPS), a provider-side control baseline for the mail-forwarder configuration surface exposed by domain registrars, shared-hosting control panels, and other operators of RFC 5321 mail-forwarding features. SMFPS defines eight normative requirements, each paired with a conformance test, whose adoption eliminates the "silent-forwarder" primitive — the capacity to redirect a mailbox's traffic to an arbitrary external destination without notifying the mailbox owner. SMFPS is complementary to RFC 7489 (DMARC) and RFC 8617 (ARC): where those documents govern the authenticity of forwarded messages, SMFPS governs the authorisation of the forwarding configuration itself.

section.name: Introduction
section.t: Email forwarding is a widely deployed feature in domain-registrar and shared-hosting product lines, in which an administrator of a domain may configure a per-mailbox or catch-all rule that redirects messages delivered at that domain to an arbitrary external destination. In the dominant deployments observed in the field, such a configuration can be added without notifying the mailbox owner, without any proof-of- ownership of the destination, and without creating an audit trail visible to the account owner. The combined effect — silent, unaudited, unnotified redirection of a mailbox's traffic — is referred to in the companion paper as the silent-forwarder primitive.

The security consequence of the primitive is disproportionate to its operational simplicity. Because email is the recovery channel for essentially every consumer and enterprise identity service, a silent forwarder constitutes a persistent, invisible account-takeover posture against every account whose recovery flow terminates at the affected mailbox.

This document specifies an interoperable baseline of eight provider- side controls, SMFPS, that, when adopted by a mail-forwarder operator, eliminates the silent-forwarder primitive while preserving legitimate forwarding use-cases.

section.name: Requirements Notation
section.t: The key words "MUST", "MUST NOT", "REQUIRED", "SHALL", "SHALL NOT", "SHOULD", "SHOULD NOT", "RECOMMENDED", "NOT RECOMMENDED", "MAY", and "OPTIONAL" in this document are to be interpreted as described in BCP 14 when, and only when, they appear in all capitals, as shown here.

dl.dd: A configured rule at the provider that causes mail addressed to a mailbox M at domain D to be re-sent to an address A outside the delivery authority of D. The tuple (D, M, A) uniquely identifies a forwarder for the purposes of this document.
The mailbox M whose mail is subject to a forwarder; the party whose correspondence is being redirected.
The natural or legal person recorded by the provider as the account holder of the registrar, hosting, or control-panel account under which the forwarder is configured.
The authenticated identity at the provider configuration plane responsible for a forwarder lifecycle event. Includes the account owner, reseller principals, API keys, and provider support staff.

section.name: Scope
section.t: SMFPS applies to any operator of an RFC 5321 mail-forwarding feature whose configuration surface is exposed to a configuring principal distinct from, or indistinct from, the owner-of-record of the affected mailboxes. This includes but is not limited to: domain- registrar bundled forwarders, hosting-control-panel forwarders (cPanel/WHM, Plesk, DirectAdmin, ISPConfig, and derivatives), and third-party mail-gateway appliances that expose a forwarder configuration surface.

SMFPS does not apply to end-user mail filtering rules configured inside an authenticated web-mail session by the mailbox owner themselves (e.g., Gmail or Outlook filter rules created by the signed-in user). Such configuration is already subject to the authentication boundary of the mail provider.

section.name: Normative Requirements
section.t: This section specifies eight normative requirements. Compliance with all eight constitutes SMFPS Full Compliance. Compliance with the subset {R1, R2, R3, R4} constitutes SMFPS Minimum Compliance; see .

section.name: R1 — Out-of-band Notification on Change
section.t: A provider MUST deliver a notification to the owner-of-record within fifteen (15) minutes of any forwarder lifecycle event (add, modify, remove). The notification MUST be delivered to a destination separate from the mail stream subject to the forwarder; permitted channels include SMS, authenticator-application push, and an alternative mailbox collected and verified at account provisioning.

Conformance: a signed test message is produced at the moment of the change; receipt at the owner-of-record out-of-band channel is verifiable from message headers or vendor delivery receipt within the fifteen-minute SLA.

section.name: R2 — Destination-Ownership Proof
section.t: A provider MUST require the forwarding destination to acknowledge the forwarder by HTTPS fetch of a per-forwarder unique URL within seven (7) days of forwarder creation, before any mail is actually forwarded. The URL MUST have at least 128 bits of entropy and MUST expire on first successful fetch or on expiry of the seven-day window, whichever is sooner.
Conformance: the first message directed to a newly-configured forwarder is held or dropped unless the acknowledgement URL has been fetched; the audit log (R4) records the acknowledgement event.

section.name: R3 — Confirmation to the Primary Mailbox
section.t: In addition to R1, a provider MUST send a confirmation message to the primary mailbox summarising the change and offering a one-click revocation URL. The revocation URL MUST remain valid for at least thirty (30) days after the configuration event. The confirmation MUST be delivered no later than the first forwarded message.
Conformance: the primary mailbox receives, no later than its first forwarded message, a message that unambiguously identifies the configuration change and offers a working revocation link.

section.name: R4 — Immutable, Principal-Attributed Audit Log
section.t: A provider MUST maintain an append-only audit log of all forwarder lifecycle events. Each entry MUST attribute the event to the configuring principal, MUST include the originating IP address, user-agent, and session identifier, and MUST NOT be mutable from the account owner's user interface.

Conformance: a sequence of forwarder lifecycle events is reflected in the log in order; an attempted deletion of an entry via the account-owner UI is rejected; a provider-side tamper of an entry is detectable by the mechanism of R5 (hash-chain or signature).

section.name: R5 — Audit Log API and Schema
section.t: A provider MUST expose the audit log of R4 through an authenticated HTTPS JSON API endpoint queryable by the account owner. The response format MUST conform to the SMFPS Audit Event schema specified in . Events MUST carry tamper-evidence in the form of a hash chain or a signature, as specified in Section .6 of the schema.
Conformance: a provided test harness enumerates events across a time window; responses validate against the schema; a tampered entry is detected by chain verification.

section.name: R6 — Per-Domain Forwarder Ceiling
section.t: A provider MUST enforce a configurable, published upper bound on the number of forwarders a single domain may host. The default ceiling MUST NOT exceed ten (10) times the number of mailboxes at the domain. Attempts to exceed the ceiling MUST be rejected with an HTTP 429-equivalent response AND MUST generate the notifications required by R1 and R3.
Conformance: a configuration attempt that would create the (N+1)th forwarder, where N is the current ceiling, is rejected; a notification is dispatched; an audit entry is written.

section.name: R7 — Loop and Chain Detection
section.t: A provider MUST detect, at the configuration-apply step, a configuration that would introduce a mail-forwarder loop (A → B → A) or a chain of depth greater than three (A → B → C → D), and MUST refuse to apply such configuration. The account owner MAY explicitly request a higher chain-depth limit through an interactive confirmation flow.
Conformance: a test suite that attempts to configure a two-hop, three-hop, four-hop, and loop configuration is rejected or respectively accepted per the above.

section.name: R8 — Reseller Attribution
section.t: Where a configuration event is initiated by a reseller, sub-account, or managed-services principal distinct from the owner-of-record, the audit log entry MUST record the full principal chain, and the notifications of R1 and R3 MUST additionally identify the reseller principal responsible.

Conformance: a reseller-provisioned API key or sub-account credential issuing a forwarder lifecycle event produces an audit entry whose principal_chain field exhibits the full delegation sequence; notifications identify the reseller.

section.name: Deployment Profiles
section.t: Two conformance profiles are defined:

dl.dd: R1, R2, R3, and R4. Appropriate for small operators (boutique registrars, single-tenant hosting providers) whose operational complexity does not justify the full control baseline. Minimum Compliance eliminates the silent-forwarder primitive but does not by itself address bulk-add, loop, or reseller-shadowing attack classes.
All of R1–R8. Appropriate for top-ten registrars, multi-tenant hosting providers at scale, and any provider offering a reseller programme.

section.name: Interactions with Other Standards
section.t: SMFPS and ARC are complementary: ARC permits a receiving MTA to reason about the authentication state of a message that has already been forwarded, while SMFPS constrains the authorisation surface by which forwarders are created. SMFPS does not supersede the sender-authentication stack SPF/DKIM/DMARC ; it occupies a strictly adjacent policy gap at the configuration plane. The research motivating this specification is reported in ; the closest prior measurement work is .
Providers MAY expose the audit log of R5 through the SCIM 2.0 event reporting extension to maximise reuse of existing enterprise-identity tooling.

section.name: Security Considerations
section.t: A provider that implements SMFPS still remains subject to attack classes against the configuration plane itself: credential theft of the account owner (defeated by MFA, outside the scope of this document), compromise of the provider's own notification path (R1 channel), and compromise of the audit log substrate (R4 / R5). Implementers are expected to deploy MFA at account provisioning, to operate the out-of-band channel of R1 on infrastructure independent of the mail-forwarder plane, and to tamper-evidence the audit log with cryptographic chaining as specified in .

Attackers may attempt to flood the R1 and R3 notification channels with legitimate configuration changes in order to desensitise the account owner. The R6 ceiling and the R1 notification rate-limit (not specified by this document; recommended at one notification per change event with per-hour aggregation above a provider-chosen threshold) mitigate this.

section.name: IANA Considerations
section.t: This document requests no IANA actions in its present form. A future revision may propose a registry for the "forwardguard" extension field of the audit event schema in .
